title: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru vs. State of Kerala
presidingJudges: Chief Justice S.M. Sikri, Justice J.M. Shelat, Justice K.S. Hegde, Justice A.N. Grover, Justice H.R. Khanna
respondent: State of Kerala & Union of India
factsSynopsis: The petitioner, head of a religious math in Kerala, challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, which imposed state restrictions on the management of religious property. While proceedings were pending, Parliament enacted the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments, which curtailed fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 and placed the state land enactments into the Ninth Schedule to immunize them from judicial review. The petitioner challenged the unconditional amending power of Parliament under Article 368.
legalIssues: Whether Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is unlimited and unfettered, or whether there exist inherent structural limitations preventing Parliament from abrogating the core identity and basic framework of the Constitution.
statutesCited: Article 368, Article 13, Article 14, Article 19, Article 31, Article 31C Constitution of India
precedentsCited: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967) 2 SCR 762; Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951)
ratioDecidendi: Parliament has wide power to amend any provision of the Constitution under Article 368, but this power does not extend to altering, damaging, or destroying the Basic Structure or essential framework of the Constitution. Judicial review, separation of powers, democracy, and fundamental rights form immutable pillars of the basic structure.
sentenceOrDamages: 25th Amendment § 3 Struck Down; Basic Structure Doctrine Established
keyTags: Basic Structure Doctrine, Article 368, Judicial Review, Constitutional Amendments, Fundamental Rights

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Chief Justice J.S. Khehar, Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice S.A. Bobde, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, Justice R.F. Nariman
petitioner: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Former High Court Judge)
respondent: Union of India & Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI)
factsSynopsis: A retired High Court judge challenged the mandatory implementation of the Aadhaar biometric identity scheme. The Union Government contended before the court that the Indian Constitution does not explicitly recognize or guarantee an independent fundamental right to privacy, citing old pre-Charter precedents.
legalIssues: Whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution of India, intrinsically linked to the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21.
statutesCited: Article 21, Article 19, Article 14 Constitution of India, Aadhaar Act 2016
precedentsCited: M.P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra (1954) SCR 1077; Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964) 1 SCR 332; Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
ratioDecidendi: The Right to Privacy is a fundamental and inalienable right protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III. Any state intrusion into personal privacy or informational self-determination must strictly satisfy the 3-fold proportionality test: legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality.
sentenceOrDamages: Unanimous Declaration of Fundamental Right to Privacy; Proportionality Standard Mandated
keyTags: Right to Privacy, Article 21, Biometrics, Informational Privacy, Proportionality Standard

title: Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Chief Justice M.H. Beg, Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, Justice P.N. Bhagwati, Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer
respondent: Union of India & Regional Passport Officer, New Delhi
factsSynopsis: The petitioner's passport was impounded by the passport authorities under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act in the 'public interest' without providing any reasons or opportunity of a prior hearing. The petitioner filed a writ petition alleging arbitrary executive deprivation of personal liberty and right to travel abroad.
legalIssues: Whether the procedure established by law under Article 21 must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating natural justice, and whether Articles 14, 19, and 21 operate as an interconnected golden triangle.
statutesCited: Article 21, Article 14, Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(1)(g) Constitution of India, Passports Act 1967 § 10(3)(c)
precedentsCited: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) SCR 88; Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1964)
ratioDecidendi: Procedure established by law under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive; it must be just, fair, and reasonable, implicitly embodying the principles of natural justice (Audi Alteram Partem). Articles 14, 19, and 21 form an indivisible Golden Triangle.
sentenceOrDamages: Impounding Order Quashed; Natural Justice Mandated for Executive Liberty Restrictions
keyTags: Golden Triangle, Natural Justice, Article 21, Due Process, Right to Travel, Arbitrary Action

title: Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Justice J. Chelameswar, Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman
petitioner: Shreya Singhal (Law Student & Free Speech Advocates)
respondent: Union of India (Ministry of Communications and IT)
factsSynopsis: Police arrested two young women under Section 66A of the Information Technology Act for posting and liking critical commentary on social media regarding a citywide shutdown. Multiple public interest petitions challenged the vague and overbroad statutory language of Section 66A, which criminalized sending 'offensive' or 'annoying' electronic messages.
legalIssues: Whether Section 66A of the IT Act violates the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) due to vagueness and chilling effect.
statutesCited: Section 66A, Section 69A, Section 79 Information Technology Act 2000, Article 19(1)(a), Article 19(2)
precedentsCited: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras (1950); Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar (1962); Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969)
ratioDecidendi: Section 66A of the IT Act is unconstitutional in its entirety. The provision creates a chilling effect on legitimate free speech and is not saved by reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). A clear distinction exists between discussion, advocacy, and incitement.
sentenceOrDamages: Section 66A IT Act Struck Down as Unconstitutional; Section 79 Safe Harbor Clarified
keyTags: Section 66A IT Act, Free Speech Online, Article 19(1)(a), Chilling Effect, Intermediary Liability

title: Navtej Singh Johar & Ors. vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Chief Justice Dipak Misra, Justice R.F. Nariman, Justice A.M. Khanwilkar, Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, Justice Indu Malhotra
petitioner: Navtej Singh Johar, Sunil Mehra, Aman Nath & LGBTQ+ Advocates
respondent: Union of India (Ministry of Law and Justice)
factsSynopsis: Members of the LGBTQ+ community filed writ petitions seeking declaration that Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, which criminalized consensual sexual acts between adults of the same sex in private, violated Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
legalIssues: Whether criminalizing consensual sexual conduct between consenting adults in private violates the constitutional guarantee of equality, dignity, privacy, and non-discrimination.
statutesCited: Section 377 Indian Penal Code 1860, Article 14, Article 15, Article 19(1)(a), Article 21 Constitution
precedentsCited: Suresh Kumar Koushal v. Naz Foundation (2014) 1 SCC 1; K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) 10 SCC 1; NALSA v. Union of India (2014)
ratioDecidendi: Section 377 IPC is unconstitutional insofar as it criminalizes consensual sexual conduct between adults in private. Constitutional morality supersedes majoritarian social morality. The rights to equality, liberty, and personal dignity protect sexual orientation.
sentenceOrDamages: Section 377 IPC Decriminalized for Consensual Adult Conduct; Koushal Verdict Overruled
keyTags: Decriminalization of Section 377, Constitutional Morality, LGBTQ+ Rights, Dignity, Article 21

title: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc. vs. Goldsmith
courtName: Supreme Court of the United States
presidingJudges: Justice Sonia Sotomayor (Majority), Chief Justice John Roberts, Justice Elena Kagan (Dissent)
petitioner: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Inc.
factsSynopsis: Photographer Lynn Goldsmith licensed a black-and-white portrait of musician Prince to Vanity Fair for an artist reference. Andy Warhol created a silkscreen illustration based on the photograph. Decades later, the Warhol Foundation licensed the silkscreen image to Condé Nast for a tribute magazine cover for $10,000 without Goldsmith's permission. The Foundation claimed Fair Use under Copyright Act § 107.
legalIssues: Whether the first fair use factor (purpose and character of the use) favors an artist foundation when both the original photograph and secondary artwork are licensed for commercial magazine publications.
statutesCited: 17 U.S. Code § 106 (Exclusive Rights), 17 U.S. Code § 107 (Fair Use Factors)
precedentsCited: Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994); Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 141 S. Ct. 1164 (2021)
ratioDecidendi: Under the first fair use factor, the commercial licensing of a secondary work to illustrate a magazine article sharing the same commercial objective as the original work does not constitute transformative fair use, even if the secondary work conveys new artistic expression.
sentenceOrDamages: Fair Use Defense Rejected; Commercial Licensing Infringement Affirmed
keyTags: Copyright, Fair Use, Transformative Work, First Factor, Derivative Works, Licensing

title: Google LLC vs. Oracle America, Inc.
courtName: Supreme Court of the United States
presidingJudges: Justice Stephen Breyer (Majority), Justice Clarence Thomas (Dissent)
factsSynopsis: Google copied approximately 11,500 lines of declaring code from 37 Java SE API packages to create the Android mobile operating system, enabling programmers familiar with Java to write applications for Android. Oracle sued Google for billions in copyright damages for verbatim copying of API declarations and structure, sequence, and organization.
legalIssues: Whether computer software application programming interface (API) declaring code is copyrightable, and whether reimplementing API declaring code for mobile software interoperability constitutes statutory Fair Use.
precedentsCited: Lotus Development Corp. v. Borland Int'l, Inc., 516 U.S. 233 (1996); Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, 510 U.S. 569 (1994)
ratioDecidendi: Google's copying of the Java SE declaring code was a fair use as a matter of law. Reimplementation included only what was necessary to allow programmers to utilize their accumulated knowledge in a new and transformative smartphone environment.
sentenceOrDamages: Fair Use Upheld as Matter of Law; Federal Circuit Reversed ($9B Claim Dismissed)
keyTags: Software Copyright, API Declaring Code, Interoperability, Fair Use, Android, Software Engineering

title: Vodafone International Holdings B.V. vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Chief Justice S.H. Kapadia, Justice K.S. Radhakrishnan, Justice Swatanter Kumar
respondent: Union of India & Assistant Director of Income Tax (International Taxation)
factsSynopsis: Vodafone (Netherlands) acquired 100% share capital of CGP Investments (Cayman Islands) from Hutchison Telecommunications for $11.1 billion, which indirectly held a 67% controlling interest in Hutchison Essar (an Indian telecom operator). Indian tax authorities raised a capital gains tax demand of ₹12,000 Crore (~$2.2B) under Section 9(1)(i) of the Income Tax Act.
legalIssues: Whether the offshore transfer of shares in a foreign holding company between two non-resident entities is subject to capital gains tax in India under Section 9(1)(i) when underlying assets reside in India.
statutesCited: Section 9(1)(i), Section 195, Section 201 Income Tax Act 1961
precedentsCited: McDowell & Co. Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer (1985) 3 SCC 230; Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan (2004)
ratioDecidendi: The 'Look At' principle applies to bona fide corporate structuring rather than 'Look Through'. Unless a transaction is a fraudulent tax sham, transfer of shares of an overseas entity cannot be deemed a transfer of underlying domestic capital assets without specific statutory look-through legislation.
sentenceOrDamages: ₹12,000 Crore Tax Demand Quashed; Look-At Doctrine Affirmed
keyTags: International Taxation, Indirect Transfer of Shares, Capital Gains, Look-At Doctrine, Corporate Structuring

title: Uber BV and Others vs. Aslam and Others
courtName: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
presidingJudges: Lord Leggatt, Lord Reed, Lady Hale, Lord Hodge, Lady Arden
petitioner: Uber BV, Uber London Ltd & Uber Britannia Ltd
respondent: Yaseen Aslam, James Farrar & Uber Drivers Union
factsSynopsis: Rideshare drivers operating on the Uber platform claimed entitlement to statutory national minimum wage, paid annual leave, and rest breaks. Uber argued that drivers were independent self-employed contractors who entered into bilateral contracts with passengers, with Uber acting solely as a booking software agent.
legalIssues: Whether gig economy app-based rideshare drivers are 'workers' within the meaning of Section 230(3)(b) of the Employment Rights Act 1996 based on statutory reality rather than contractual labels.
statutesCited: Employment Rights Act 1996 § 230(3)(b), National Minimum Wage Act 1998, Working Time Regulations 1998
precedentsCited: Autoclenz Ltd v. Belcher [2011] UKSC 41; Carmichael v. National Power plc [1999] 1 WLR 2042
ratioDecidendi: Employment classification must be determined by reference to statutory purpose and actual subordination rather than formalistic written contractual documentation. Because Uber exercises extensive algorithmic control over pricing, performance ratings, and ride allocations, drivers are statutory workers.
sentenceOrDamages: Driver Worker Status Affirmed; Entitlement to Minimum Wage and Holiday Pay Mandated
keyTags: Gig Economy, Worker Status, Algorithmic Control, Minimum Wage, Employment Rights, Subordination

title: M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case)
presidingJudges: Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati, Justice Ranganath Misra, Justice G.L. Oza, Justice M.M. Dutt, Justice K.N. Singh
respondent: Union of India & Shriram Foods & Fertilizer Industries
factsSynopsis: In December 1985, a catastrophic leak of hazardous oleum gas occurred at the Shriram Foods and Fertilizer plant in New Delhi, killing an advocate and causing serious respiratory distress to thousands of residents. The company sought to evade strict liability under the 1868 Rylands v. Fletcher rule by pleading third-party maintenance fault and statutory exceptions.
legalIssues: Whether an industrial enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities is subject to Absolute Liability without any exceptions or defenses recognized under common law strict liability.
statutesCited: Article 21, Article 32 Constitution of India, Water & Air Pollution Control Acts
ratioDecidendi: An enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous industry owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. If harm results, the enterprise is absolutely liable to compensate all affected parties without exception (no defense of act of God, third-party act, or absence of negligence).
sentenceOrDamages: Doctrine of Absolute Liability Established; Mandatory Compensation Fund Mandated
keyTags: Absolute Liability, Hazardous Industry, Polluter Pays, Article 21, Industrial Disaster, Environmental Tort

title: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum vs. Union of India
presidingJudges: Justice Kuldip Singh, Justice Faizan Uddin, Justice K. Venkataswami
respondent: Union of India, State of Tamil Nadu & 900+ Tanneries
factsSynopsis: Hundreds of tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated toxic effluents containing chromium into the Palar River basin, contaminating 35,000 hectares of agricultural land and rendering groundwater non-potable for over 100 villages.
legalIssues: Whether the Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principle are integral parts of environmental law under Article 21 and customary international law.
statutesCited: Article 21, Article 47, Article 48A, Article 51A(g) Constitution, Environment (Protection) Act 1986 § 3, § 5
precedentsCited: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) 3 SCC 212; Rio Declaration 1992 Principle 15
ratioDecidendi: The Precautionary Principle and the Polluter Pays Principle are essential features of Sustainable Development and form part of the law of the land under Article 21. The polluter is liable not only to compensate victims but also to pay the complete costs of environmental ecological restoration.
sentenceOrDamages: ₹10,000 Fine per Tannery + Complete Ecological Remediation Assessment Mandated
keyTags: Precautionary Principle, Polluter Pays Principle, Sustainable Development, Water Pollution, Tanneries

title: Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab
presidingJudges: Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, Justice A.C. Gupta, Justice N.L. Untwalia, Justice P.N. Bhagwati (Dissent)
factsSynopsis: The appellant was convicted of triple murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of capital punishment under Section 302 IPC read with Section 354(3) CrPC as violating Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution.
legalIssues: Whether the death penalty prescribed under Section 302 IPC violates fundamental rights, and what judicial standards govern the exercise of discretion in awarding capital punishment.
statutesCited: Section 302 Indian Penal Code, Section 354(3) Code of Criminal Procedure 1973, Article 21 Constitution
precedentsCited: Jagmohan Singh v. State of U.P. (1973) 1 SCC 20; Rajendra Prasad v. State of U.P. (1979) 3 SCC 646
ratioDecidendi: The death penalty does not violate Article 14, 19, or 21 if awarded under a fair procedure. However, the extreme penalty of death must be restricted strictly to the 'Rarest of Rare cases' where the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed. Courts must balance aggravating and mitigating circumstances.
sentenceOrDamages: Death Sentence Commuted to Life Imprisonment; 'Rarest of Rare' Doctrine Formulated
keyTags: Death Penalty, Rarest of Rare, Section 302 IPC, Section 354(3) CrPC, Sentencing Discretion, Article 21

title: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda vs. State of Maharashtra
presidingJudges: Justice S. Murtaza Fazal Ali, Justice A. Varadarajan, Justice Sabyasachi Mukharji
factsSynopsis: The appellant was convicted of poisoning and murdering his newly married wife based entirely on circumstantial evidence and dying declarations. The High Court affirmed the death sentence. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court arguing the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and consistent with suicide.
legalIssues: What are the cardinal legal principles ('Panchsheel') governing convictions based solely on circumstantial evidence in criminal trials under the Indian Evidence Act.
statutesCited: Section 302 IPC, Section 32(1), Section 3 Indian Evidence Act 1872
precedentsCited: Hanumant v. State of M.P. (1952) SCR 1091; Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra (1973)
ratioDecidendi: Conviction on circumstantial evidence requires five golden principles ('Panchsheel'): (1) circumstances from which guilt is drawn must be fully established, (2) facts established must be consistent only with guilt, (3) circumstances must be conclusive, (4) they must exclude every hypothesis of innocence, and (5) chain of evidence must be complete without gaps.
sentenceOrDamages: Death Sentence Quashed; Appellant Acquitted of All Murder Charges
keyTags: Circumstantial Evidence, Panchsheel of Circumstantial Evidence, Section 302 IPC, Dying Declaration, Chain of Custody

title: Shayara Bano vs. Union of India & Ors. (Triple Talaq)
presidingJudges: Chief Justice J.S. Khehar, Justice Kurian Joseph, Justice Rohinton F. Nariman, Justice U.U. Lalit, Justice S. Abdul Nazeer
petitioner: Shayara Bano & Muslim Women Quest for Equality
respondent: Union of India, Ministry of Law & All India Muslim Personal Law Board
factsSynopsis: Petitioner was summarily divorced through instantaneous and irrevocable Talaq-e-Biddat (Triple Talaq) by her husband after 15 years of marriage. She filed a writ petition challenging the practice of Triple Talaq, polygamy, and nikah halala as violative of Articles 14, 15, 21, and 25 of the Constitution.
legalIssues: Whether the practice of Talaq-e-Biddat (instant Triple Talaq) is protected under Article 25 freedom of religion as an essential religious practice, or whether it is manifestly arbitrary and unconstitutional under Article 14.
statutesCited: Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 § 2, Article 14, Article 21, Article 25 Constitution
precedentsCited: Shamim Ara v. State of U.P. (2002) 7 SCC 518; Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995)
ratioDecidendi: Talaq-e-Biddat is manifestly arbitrary because it allows a marital tie to be severed capriciously without any attempt at reconciliation. Manifest arbitrariness is a recognized ground to invalidate statutory provisions and customary personal law rules under Article 14.
sentenceOrDamages: Practice of Talaq-e-Biddat Declared Void and Unconstitutional by 3:2 Majority
keyTags: Triple Talaq, Talaq-e-Biddat, Manifest Arbitrariness, Article 14, Gender Equality, Muslim Personal Law

title: Vineeta Sharma vs. Rakesh Sharma & Ors.
presidingJudges: Justice Arun Mishra, Justice S. Abdul Nazeer, Justice M.R. Shah
factsSynopsis: Conflicting judgments of the Supreme Court existed regarding whether the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 conferred equal coparcenary birthrights to daughters if the coparcener father had died prior to the date of the amendment (September 9, 2005).
legalIssues: Whether the substituted Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act confers coparcenary status on daughters by birth retrospectively or prospectively, and whether the father must be alive on the amendment date.
statutesCited: Section 6 Hindu Succession Act 1956 (as amended by Act 39 of 2005)
precedentsCited: Prakash v. Phulavati (2016) 2 SCC 36; Danamma v. Amar (2018) 3 SCC 343
ratioDecidendi: A daughter is born with equal coparcenary rights in ancestral Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) property in the same manner as a son. The right is conferred by birth and is not dependent on the coparcener father being alive on the date of the 2005 amendment.
sentenceOrDamages: Equal Coparcenary Birthright of Daughters Affirmed; Prakash v. Phulavati Overruled
keyTags: Hindu Succession Act § 6, Coparcenary Rights, Gender Equality in Inheritance, Ancestral Property
